title: Reading Royal Names
short: Read a cartouche sign by sign, remembering honorific transposition: jmn written first in Tutankhamun is read last.
trouble: Students read the god's name first because it is written first.

blocks.html: Time to read real royal names. Everything you have learned comes together: sound signs (The Alphabet V: t ṯ d ḏ), biliterals and triliterals, determinatives, and above all honorific transposition, which turns up in most names that contain a god (Cartouches and Their Titles).

Read a cartouche sign by sign, then check for a god’s name written first. In twt-ꜥnḫ-jmn Tutankhamun, Amun’s name is written first but read last; in jmn-ḥtp Amenhotep it is read first, because it belongs first.

blocks.name: eg-cartouche
blocks.cap: Ramesses: the sun rꜥ, the fox skins ms, and the folded cloth s twice. Champollion read this name in 1822.

blocks.html: Under the Ptolemies, Greek names were spelled out with one-consonant signs, and a few signs took on new values: the lion 𓃭 writes l, the lasso 𓍯 an o-like sound. ptwlmys is Ptolemy and qljwpꜣdrꜣt Cleopatra. These were the names Young and Champollion used to start the decipherment.

Why is the god sometimes read last? Many royal names are short sentences or phrases about a god: “living image of Amun”, “enduring is the form of Ra”. Grammar puts the god at the end (“image of Amun”), but honor puts him at the front of the writing. When the god is the subject of the sentence (“Amun is content”), he comes first in both.

Reading the god’s name first because it is written first: “Amun-tut-ankh”. Translate the name: if the god is the possessor or comes after a verb or adjective in the meaning, he is read last. Check with a known name: Tutankhamun, not Amuntutankh.
